01The problem

Guwahati doesn't plan where its waste goes. It dumps it.

0
people living in the city
0t/day
of waste every day
0
wards to serve
0
protected wetland at risk

The city's waste goes to one dump at Boragaon, right next to Deepor Beel. That lake is a protected wetland, and it soaks up Guwahati's rainwater. The dump ended up there because the land was free, not because anyone checked whether it was a good spot. Now rubbish leaks into the lake, and trucks cross the whole city every day to reach it.

02Energy from waste

Three ways to turn rubbish into power.

Waste can be burned, eaten by tiny microbes, or buried. Each of these can make energy. Pick one to see how it works and whether it suits Guwahati.

03Guwahati's plan

Not one big furnace. Five smart hubs.

Almost half of Guwahati's waste is wet food scraps, and wet waste doesn't burn well. So instead of burning everything, we sort it and send each kind where it's most useful. Here's where the city's 458 tonnes go each day.

04How we score land

Eight questions for every spot in the city.

Is it far from water? Safe from floods? Close to the waste and the roads? We asked eight questions like these for every 30 m square of Guwahati. A method called AHP decides how much each question counts by comparing them two at a time, and a built-in check confirms the choices agree with each other.

    08Results

    Five sites. Half the driving.

    Once all the off-limits land is removed, very little of Guwahati is left. The model finds five open plots at the edge of the city. Together they cut daily truck driving by about half compared with taking everything to Boragaon.

    Why land is off-limits

    Driving is measured in a straight line from each ward's centre to its nearest site, multiplied by tonnes. Boragaon is the dump's real location. Power access uses 11 substations we mapped by hand. A spot can be off-limits for more than one reason, so the shares add up to more than 100%.

    09Power link

    Making power is useless if it can't get out.

    A substation changes the voltage of electricity so it can travel and then be used safely at home. It's also the door a small plant uses to send its power into the city. So for every possible site we asked one question: how far is the nearest door? We mapped 11 substations around Guwahati to find out.

    How far each hub is from its substation
    2.5 km: about as far as a cable is worth building
    ₹

    It pays the bills

    Selling electricity brings in money every day. That money pays the workers and trucks that treat the waste. Hubs that only cost money tend to shut down, and the waste goes back to the dump.

    ⚡

    It keeps the hub running

    The hub's own shredders, pumps and belts need steady power, even on days when its generator is down for repairs.

    7%

    It's a helper, not the main goal

    A substation never touches waste. That's why it counts for only 7% of the score. Safety from water and floods counts for 24% each.

    What we add

    • Plans a network of five sites and which wards each one serves, not a single dump.
    • Uses where people live, so the sites end up close to the waste.
    • Builds its own flood map for the Brahmaputra floodplain.
    • Picks the treatment that suits the waste: gas plants and fuel, not burning.
    • Lets anyone change the weights and see the result straight away.

    What we'd add next

    • Ask experts to set the weights, as Mostafa et al. did with 42 specialists.
    • Test the results against real sites and check how much the weights matter.
    • Use real road distances and plant size limits instead of straight lines.
    • Look beyond city limits: Hazarika & Saikia's best site is in North Guwahati.
    11Limitations

    What this study can't tell you yet.

    This is a first look, not a final answer. Here is what we could not check yet, and what would fix it.

    01

    We chose the weights

    We decided how much each factor counts. No experts were asked yet.

    Fix: Ask experts
    02

    Not tested yet

    We haven't checked the results against real plants.

    Fix: Test the results
    03

    Straight-line distances

    We measured distance in a straight line, not along roads.

    Fix: Use real road routes
    04

    Waste is estimated

    We worked out waste from population: 0.4 kg per person a day.

    Fix: Use the city's truck records
    05

    Our own flood map

    We made the flood map ourselves. It isn't an official one.

    Fix: Compare with real flood records
    06

    Only inside the city

    Land just outside the city limits wasn't checked.

    Fix: Map a bigger area
    07

    Substation size unknown

    We don't know how much extra power each substation can take.

    Fix: Ask the power company
    08

    Owners not checked

    Some open plots may be private or already in use.

    Fix: Check land records
    09

    Borrowed numbers

    Some figures come from other places, like Indore's plant.

    Fix: Run a small test plant
    12Impact

    What changes for the city.

    NATURE

    Protects wetlands

    No new site goes near Deepor Beel, flood zones or homes.

    MONEY

    Cheaper collection

    Shorter trips mean less fuel, lower costs and cleaner air.

    ENERGY

    Waste becomes fuel

    Food scraps become gas for vehicles. Dry waste replaces coal.

    TRUST

    Easy to explain

    The city can show exactly why each site was picked.

    REUSE

    Works elsewhere

    Any growing, flood-prone city in the Northeast can use the same method.

    MONSOON

    Runs in the rain

    Sites stay out of flood zones, so they keep working through the monsoon.
